title: Toronto hostage-taker's gun was jammed
article: The sawed-off.22-calibre rifle used by 45-year-old Sugston Anthony Brookes in the Union Station standoff on Wednesday had jammed before he held it to his hostage's head, a police source says.

The semi-automatic weapon "stovepiped" - jamming after a spent casing was only partially ejected from the chamber - after Mr. Brookes fired two shots at his estranged wife in a food court below the TD Centre, minutes before he was spotted on Front Street.

Word of the jam, which may have spared the life of Mr. Brookes's wife as well as that of 20-year-old hostage Nicole Regis, comes after reports that investigators found a rambling, five-minute taped message from Mr. Brookes to his wife when they searched his van, which was found parked downtown on Lombard Street.

On the tape, possibly recorded while he drove downtown from his Ajax home, Mr. Brookes blames his estranged wife for his actions, a police source said. "You made me do this.... You drove me to it," the taped message says.

Mr. Brookes did not spell out his violent plan on the tape, but police assumed from what he said that several scenarios were possible, from killing his estranged wife to shooting police and bystanders.
After he fired two shots at his wife, she tripped and fell. Mr. Brookes then beat her around the head and fled. Minutes later he was outside Union Station with Ms. Regis as a hostage.

Meanwhile, the unnamed police officer who fired the shot that killed Mr. Brookes is said to be distressed after the incident, but is receiving support and counsel from other police officers and officials with the Toronto Police Association.
The province's Special Investigations Unit, probing the shooting of Mr. Brookes, said it was starting to interview some of the police officers who saw what happened.

Spokeswoman Rose Bliss said the SIU has now designated 19 witness officers who are obligated to co-operate with the SIU, and two subject officers, whose actions are being investigated and who are not required to submit to interviews.

In this case, the two subject officers are members of the Emergency Task Force tactical unit. One is the sharpshooter who pulled the trigger, the other the supervisor who authorized the use of deadly force, she said.
"This is not a case of a whodunit scenario - it's how did it happen? Why did it happen?" Ms. Bliss said.
She couldn't say how long the investigation would take, but said that last year, more than half of the SIU's probes took less than a month.

Once the investigation is complete, it is up to the James Cornish, the SIU's interim director, to decide whether charges against the subject officers should be laid. The SIU investigates all police incidents that result in serious injury or death.

Most of the witness officers will have lawyers present, paid for by the Toronto Police Association, for their SIU interviews. Legal help, if needed, and counselling are also being provided to the two subject officers.

Chief Coroner Barry McLellan said the postmortem on Mr. Brookes's body was completed yesterday morning and confirmed that the man died instantly from a single gunshot wound to the head. But it could take a couple of weeks before other tests to determine whether Mr. Brookes had alcohol or drugs in his bloodstream are completed.

Dr. McLellan said his office was gathering information about the man's history of domestic violence. But any decision on whether to call a full-scale coroner's inquest into the shooting was likely weeks away.

"First of all we need to allow the SIU to complete their investigation. Then it is in our hands," Dr. McLellan said. Any future coroner's inquest could look at both the police shooting and at how the system dealt with Mr. Brookes before his death, he added.
Yesterday, Ontario Court Judge Gregory Regis, whose daughter was the young woman taken hostage in the incident, said the family "needed time" before they could speak with reporters.
Ms. Regis was a summer employee at the Royal Bank and is reportedly a student at McMaster University in Hamilton.

In a statement issued by a family spokesman, the Regis family thanked police, emergency services and medical staff who assisted their daughter and indicated that "Nicole is doing well and is resting at home."
The family, who live in Ajax, also expressed "sympathy to the family of the man who was involved in this incident."
